name: Methodologies & Teamwork
description: Agile, Scrum, Kanban, waterfall, estimation, and the team practices that decide whether software ships.

modules.name: Process Models
modules.description: The frameworks, what they are actually for, and how they fail.

cards.answer: Waterfall completes each phase before the next — requirements, design, build, test, release. Agile delivers small increments repeatedly, adapting as it learns.

left.title: Waterfall
points: Feedback arrives only at the end

right.title: Agile
points: Needs an engaged customer and real autonomy

cards.explanation: Waterfall is not a mistake — it is correct where change is expensive and requirements genuinely are known (bridges, avionics, certified medical devices). Agile bets that you will learn things that invalidate the plan, which for most software is true.

cards.answer: Scrum is iteration-based with fixed-length sprints, defined roles and ceremonies. Kanban is flow-based: visualise the work, limit work in progress, and optimise cycle time — no sprints required.

left.title: Scrum
points: Product owner and scrum master roles
Cadence helps teams that need structure

right.title: Kanban
points: WIP limits are the core mechanic
Better fit for support and interrupt-driven work

cards.explanation: WIP limits are the most transferable idea in either: starting less finishes more, because context switching and queueing are what actually slow teams down. Many teams run 'Scrumban' — Scrum's cadence with Kanban's flow limits.

cards.prompt: What is each Scrum ceremony actually for?
cards.answer: Planning: agree what the sprint will deliver. Daily standup: surface blockers and re-plan the day (15 minutes, not a status report to a manager). Review: show working software to stakeholders and get feedback. Retrospective: improve how the team works.
cards.explanation: Each fails in a characteristic way: standups become status theatre, reviews become demos of slides, retros become complaint sessions with no actions. The test for any ceremony is whether it changes a decision — if not, it is a meeting with a costume on.

cards.prompt: Why are software estimates so consistently wrong, and what helps?
cards.answer: Because estimating means predicting work you have not yet understood, and the planning fallacy makes people estimate the best case. What helps: relative sizing, breaking work down until items are small, historical throughput, and giving ranges or confidence intervals rather than single numbers.
cards.explanation: Story points try to sidestep the problem by measuring relative size and letting observed velocity convert to time. The pathology is treating points as hours or as a productivity metric — at which point they get inflated and stop informing anything. Small slices beat clever estimation.

modules.name: Teams & Delivery
modules.description: How teams actually get good, measured and unblocked.

cards.prompt: What are the DORA software-delivery metrics?
cards.answer: Throughput: deployment frequency, change lead time, and failed-deployment recovery time. Instability: change failure rate and deployment rework rate (unplanned deployments made to fix user-facing problems). The original "four keys" gained rework rate as a fifth metric in 2024.
cards.explanation: The key research finding is that throughput and stability do not trade off — top performers deploy more often *and* break things less, because small frequent changes are easier to verify and revert. Measure the team's system, never individuals; any metric used to rank people becomes a target and stops measuring.

cards.prompt: What is Conway's Law, and what is the 'inverse Conway manoeuvre'?
cards.answer: Organisations design systems that mirror their communication structures. The inverse manoeuvre is deliberately reorganising teams to produce the architecture you want.
cards.explanation: Four teams on a compiler produce a four-pass compiler. If you want autonomous services, you need autonomous teams that own them end to end; if teams must coordinate for every release, your architecture will keep re-coupling no matter how you draw the diagram.

cards.prompt: What did Google's Project Aristotle find distinguishes effective teams?
cards.answer: Psychological safety — the shared belief that you can take risks, admit mistakes and ask questions without being punished — mattered more than talent, tenure or team composition.
cards.explanation: It is directly operational for engineering: safe teams report incidents early, ask 'why is this like this?' in review, and stop bad plans before they ship. Blameless post-mortems and leaders admitting uncertainty are the concrete practices that build it.

cards.prompt: What does 'technical debt' mean, and how should a team manage it?
cards.answer: A deliberate trade of long-term maintainability for short-term speed, which then charges interest as slower future changes. Manage it by making it visible, paying it down continuously alongside features, and distinguishing deliberate debt from plain mess.
cards.explanation: The metaphor only works if the debt was a decision. 'We didn't know how' is not debt, it is learning; 'we never cleaned up' is not debt, it is neglect. A dedicated 'refactoring sprint' rarely gets approved — continuous small improvement does.

cards.prompt: Which documentation is worth writing, given that all of it goes stale?
cards.answer: The kind that cannot be derived from the code: why a decision was made (ADRs), how to run and deploy the system, the architecture overview, runbooks for incidents, and API contracts for consumers. Not line-by-line descriptions of what code does.
cards.explanation: Keep docs close to the code so they are updated in the same pull request, and prefer generated documentation (OpenAPI, type-derived docs) where possible. A wrong document is worse than a missing one, so delete aggressively.

resources.title: Diátaxis — A systematic framework for technical documentation

modules.name: Planning & Delivering Work
modules.description: User stories and acceptance criteria, definition of done, prioritisation, slicing, flow and XP practices.

cards.prompt: What makes a good user story, and what are acceptance criteria for?
cards.answer: A short statement of a need from a user's perspective — "As a returning customer, I want to reorder a past purchase so that I save time" — that is Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable (INVEST). Acceptance criteria list the concrete conditions that must hold for it to be done, often as Given–When–Then examples.
cards.explanation: A story is a placeholder for a conversation, not a specification. Criteria make "done" checkable and give testers and developers a shared target; if you cannot write them, the story is not understood yet.

cards.prompt: What is a definition of done, and how does it differ from acceptance criteria?
cards.answer: A team-wide checklist every item must meet before it counts as done — code reviewed, tests written and passing, deployed to production (or releasable), documentation and monitoring updated. Acceptance criteria are specific to one story.
cards.explanation: Without a shared definition, "done" means "works on my machine" and unfinished work accumulates as hidden debt. Keep it short, visible and genuinely enforced; strengthen it as the team's practices mature.

resources.title: Scrum Guide — Increment and Definition of Done

cards.prompt: MoSCoW vs value-based scoring (RICE, WSJF) for prioritising a backlog
cards.answer: MoSCoW sorts items into Must, Should, Could and Won't (this time) — fast and good for scoping a release. RICE (Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort) and WSJF (cost of delay ÷ job size) score items numerically so they can be ranked.

right.title: RICE / WSJF
points: WSJF favours small, urgent, valuable work
False precision if inputs are guesses

cards.explanation: Numbers create an illusion of precision, but they force explicit assumptions that can be challenged. MoSCoW fails when everything becomes a Must. Whatever the method, revisit priorities as you learn — and "Won't" is the most valuable category.

resources.title: Intercom — RICE: simple prioritization for product managers

cards.prompt: A feature is split into "build the database schema", "build the API" and "build the UI" tickets, and nothing is usable for six weeks. How should it be split?
cards.answer: Into vertical slices: thin end-to-end increments that each deliver working, usable behaviour through every layer — "a user can see their last three orders" before "a user can filter orders by date". Each slice can be shipped, demonstrated and learned from.
cards.explanation: Horizontal layers defer integration risk and feedback to the end. Vertical slices surface problems early, allow reprioritising mid-feature, and pair naturally with feature flags so partial features can ship dark.

resources.title: Humanizing Work — The Humanizing Work guide to splitting user stories

cards.prompt: What is flow efficiency, and why is it usually shockingly low?
cards.answer: Active work time divided by total elapsed time for an item. For typical software teams it is often well under 20%: most of a ticket's life is spent waiting — for review, for another team, for a deploy window, for a decision.
cards.explanation: Speeding up the work itself barely helps when waiting dominates. Reduce queues instead: limit work in progress, review promptly, remove hand-offs and approval steps, and automate deployment. This is the Lean insight behind Kanban.

cards.prompt: What are the core practices of Extreme Programming (XP)?
cards.answer: Test-driven development, pair programming, continuous integration, small frequent releases, simple design, refactoring, collective code ownership, a sustainable pace, and an on-site (or constantly available) customer.
cards.explanation: Scrum describes how to organise work; XP describes how to engineer it — which is why many "agile" teams struggle when they adopt the ceremonies but not the technical practices. The DORA research later confirmed many XP practices as drivers of delivery performance.

cards.prompt: A distributed team across five time zones is drowning in meetings. How should it communicate?
cards.answer: Default to asynchronous, written communication: decisions and proposals in documents with comment periods, status in the tracker instead of meetings, recorded demos, and clear ownership. Reserve synchronous time for discussion that genuinely benefits from it — conflict, brainstorming, relationship-building.
cards.explanation: Writing things down creates a searchable record and includes people who could not attend. Explicit response-time expectations prevent constant interruption, and overlapping hours should be protected for the conversations that need them.
